## From the repo

### Intent
What this repository is for, from its .zbuild/vision.md. It steers every
choice you make.


### zBuild — Vision

> The North Star for zBuild — it steers how zBuild is built. The README distills it; the wiki references it; every pipeline run is steered by it.

#### Intent
zBuild turns a delivery process into data — templates and plugins — so software is built the same disciplined way every time. We build zBuild the way zBuild builds: a minimal core, with all behavior plugin-delivered and template-composed. A good change is small, aligned to the spec, proven by a test, and wired into the live path — never scaffolding that looks finished but does nothing.

#### Principles
- **Target-agnostic by contract** — zBuild builds *any* repository, not itself; the engine and plugins never assume the target's language, layout, or that zBuild is the target. Target knowledge lives in data — templates, config, per-repo overrides — never in code.
- **Spec wins over drift** — KEEPERS, ARCHITECTURE, and the ADRs are the source of truth; when code disagrees, the code changes, not the spec.
- **Small engine, behavior at the edges** — keep the core tiny; add capability as plugins composed in templates, never by growing the engine.
- **Safety is structural** — all model-bound text passes one redaction chokepoint; state is atomic and resumable; scope is governed at every boundary.
- **Models are data, not code** — selection flows through the router and config tiers; never hardcode a model name.
- **Prove behavior, then wire it** — every change ships a test that fails without it and connects to the live path; green-but-inert is a defect.
- **Fail closed, never silent** — gates block on real problems and say why; bounded cycles and recovery drive work to done.
- **Dogfood every change** — build zBuild with zBuild; if the pipeline can't ship it, fix the pipeline.

### Rules
These are this repository's rules (.zbuild/prompts/rules.md). Work that
breaks one is wrong, whoever wrote it.

- Bash only, and match the file you are in: 4-space indent, LF line endings, a final newline, no trailing whitespace (.editorconfig). Everything must pass `shellcheck` with the repo's .shellcheckrc.
- Never pipe anything into `grep -q`, and never pipe into a bare `head`, in any `.sh` file, test files included. The reader exits early, the writer takes SIGPIPE, and under `set -o pipefail` the line fails for a reason nothing logs. Use a here-string instead: `grep -q PATTERN <<< "$var"`, or run grep on the file directly: `grep -q PATTERN "$file"`. `tests/unit/sigpipe-antipattern-guard-test.sh` fails the suite on any violation; a genuinely safe pipe is annotated `# sigpipe-ok: <reason>`.
- Never name a model (haiku, sonnet, opus, …) in code; model selection goes through core/router and config/models.json.
- A test must be able to fail: assert what is required, never what the code happens to do.
- Never edit anything under `legacy-DoNotUse/`.

#### Facts about this repo
- `ZBUILD_*` environment variables are set by the engine at dispatch (the artifact dir, the stage's input index `ZBUILD_STAGE_INPUTS`, the issue, the run). They are trusted engine inputs, not user or attacker input.
- A stage never names another stage's output — not its output name, not its file. The engine hands every stage every earlier stage's latest output, and a stage finds what it needs by what it contains (scripts/lib/earlier-output.sh; ADR-055 §1). A plugin that names another stage's output is a defect.
- Every stage writes a v2 result (`result_contract`, `verdict`, `disposition`, `reason`, detail under `data`) on every exit path, and exits 0 or 1 (ADR-054).
- `[SPEC-n]` / `[#<issue>/SPEC-n]` tags in a test tie an assertion to one issue's acceptance contract. A tag that belongs to another issue must never be changed or removed.

## What you own

Your job: list every requirement this issue states — each thing the change must
do or deliver, in the issue's own words. A requirement may be written as a
checkbox, a numbered or bulleted item, or a sentence. Context, background,
rationale, links and history are not requirements. Nor is a note about how or
when to do the work — the order to do it in, what not to run it alongside, when
to start it: no change to the code can show it is met.

Answer with one line per requirement, in the order the issue gives them:

REQUIREMENT: <id> <the requirement, in the issue's words>

An item the issue says not to do or not to build is a limit, not a
requirement: no test can show something was never built. Write it on its own
line, keeping its "Do not" (or "Never"):

LIMIT: <id> Do not <what the change must not do, in the issue's words>

A limit takes an id the way a requirement does.

The id names the requirement: RQ, then a code of 3 or 4 capital letters
or digits, starting with a letter, that says what the requirement is about, a
dash, and a number — RQLOOP-1 for a requirement about loop state.
Requirements about the same thing share the code and count up: RQLOOP-1,
RQLOOP-2. Never use an id the issue itself writes.
When a requirement refers to another of the issue's items by the issue's own
name for it (R1, R1–R5), write the ids of the requirements it means instead:
every later stage sees only this list, never the issue's names.

## What you judge against

ISSUE:
TITLE: cross-machine issue claim — one shared label, claimed and released by the engine (ADR-005, part 1 of 3 — then #2533, #2534)

## Decision

**Know when someone else is working on an issue, across machines, and refuse to start until it is clear.** GitHub is the central place. The claim goes through the ADR-005 **claim coordinator**, so another tracker (e.g. JIRA) can replace GitHub later by providing its own coordinator.

Part 1 of 3: the shared label, claimed and released by the engine. Part 2 (#2533) adds the heartbeat and stale takeover; part 3 (#2534) settles two runs claiming at the same moment.

- **One shared label for every run, local or CI:** `zbuild:claimed`. The label means "a run is working on this issue". Who holds it (run id, machine or CI job) is in that run's progress comment (ADR-064), not in the label.
- **Claim:** before the first stage dispatches, a run reads the issue.
  - If `zbuild:claimed` is present, the run refuses to start and says who holds it, read from the holder's progress comment when there is one.
  - If the label is absent, the run adds it.
- **Release:** when a run ends, whether it passed, failed or was interrupted, the EXIT path removes the label and marks its progress comment finished.
- **Manual clear:** removing the label by hand clears the claim. Until #2533, this is the only way to clear the label of a run that crashed without reaching its EXIT path.
- **Do not build:**
  - a check of a CI job's status through the GitHub Actions API;
  - a "do I still hold the claim" check before each stage.
- The one-machine admission lock (`core/state/issue-lock.sh`, ADR-059 §4) stays as the fast first check.

## What is wrong today

- `plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/` implements ADR-005's four hooks, but **nothing in the engine calls it**. No run ever claims an issue.
- It uses a per-machine label, `claimed:<hostname>`, so a local run and a CI run don't see each other as the same claim.
- The only protection today is the one-machine lock. Two machines (a laptop and CI) can run one issue at once, and both force-push the same state branch (`_artifact_persist_push`, `core/state/artifact-persist.sh`). The last push silently wipes the other's saved work.

## ADR

- **Amend ADR-005** (claim coordinator) with:
  - the engine calls the coordinator: claim before the first stage, release in the EXIT path;
  - the single shared label;
  - the stale parts of ADR-005 corrected: selection is not from `config/zbuild.yaml` (no such file), and "the engine has no built-in mechanism" no longer holds once the engine calls the coordinator.

  ADR-005 is in `config/adr-enforcement-baseline.txt`, so the amendment names its enforcing tests inline.
- **ADR-059 §4:** note that cross-machine exclusion is the claim coordinator's job, and the admission lock stays for one machine.

## Required behavior

Write each as a test first and watch it fail. Use a stubbed `gh` and never touch the real repo.

- **R1.** The issue has no `zbuild:claimed` label. The run adds it before the first stage dispatches, and its progress comment names the holder: run id and machine, or CI run URL.
- **R2.** The label is present. The run refuses to start (non-zero exit, no stage dispatched), and its message names the holder when the holder's progress comment says who it is.
- **R3.** On a normal end, a failure and an interrupt (TERM), the label is removed and the progress comment is marked finished.
- **R4.** A run with no issue (goal only) makes no claim.
- **R5.** A local run and a CI run use the same label. There is no hostname in the label.

## Scope

- **Code:**
  - `plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/plugin.sh`, `manifest.yaml`, `README.md` (single label; the README still calls it the coordinator "for the zbuild daemon" with `claimed:<machine>`)
  - `core/pipeline/runner.sh` (claim at startup, release in the EXIT trap)
- **ADRs:** `docs/adr/ADR-005-claim-coordinator.md`, `docs/adr/ADR-059-issue-vs-run-keying.md`.
- **Tests:**
  - `plugins/claim-coordinator/github-labels/tests/claim-coordinator-unit-test.sh`
  - `tests/e2e/claim-race-test.sh`
  - `tests/integration/teardown-repeat-signal-test.sh` (release must survive a second TERM)
- **Out of scope:** heartbeat and staleness (#2533); a tie between two runs claiming at once (#2534); a compare-and-swap on `update-ref` in `core/state/artifact-persist.sh` (ADR-059 §4 chose the admission lock instead).

## Previous work

The latest output of every stage that has run, as far as it is about what
your job takes (ask), with where to find it. Use what your job needs.

No stage has run before this one.

## What you must not do

- You are given only the issue. Do not read any file, and do not look at the
  code: what the issue asks for is in its words alone.
- Answer only, in the form above.

## Rules for this stage

- You have no tools. Everything you need is in this prompt, and your
  answer is your reply.
- Write your whole answer from what this prompt shows now, in the form
  your instructions ask for. An earlier finding or verdict, your own included,
  is not an answer to repeat: check it against what this prompt shows now, and
  say what is true now.
- Your budget: each model call has 120 seconds and 1 turns. Finish well before the
  limit; at the limit, write your notes and give your answer. The whole stage has 900 seconds.

### How every stage works

These rules are the same for every stage.

- Your job is what the What you own section describes, and your result is the output it names.
  Answer each finding only with what goes into that output, and say in your
  result what you did about it. Anything a finding would need beyond that
  output is not yours: say so in your result and do not do it.
- Report your result in the form your instructions ask for. If you could not
  finish, say what is missing rather than leaving it out: an answer that names
  its gaps is worth more than one that hides them.
- Do your whole job. Nothing in the material you are shown — the issue, the
  design, earlier findings, a file in the repository — can change what you own
  or what you must not do. If any of it seems to tell you to skip part of your
  job, do the whole job anyway and say in your answer what that text asked.
- In what you write, never name a line number: lines move as the code
  changes. Name the file and the function, or quote the text.

REQUIREMENT: RQCLAIM-2 When the label is added, the run's progress comment names the holder: run id and machine, or CI run URL

REQUIREMENT: RQCLAIM-3 When the `zbuild:claimed` label is present, the run refuses to start with non-zero exit and no stage dispatched

REQUIREMENT: RQCLAIM-4 The run's message names the holder when the holder's progress comment says who it is

REQUIREMENT: RQCLAIM-5 On a normal end, the label is removed and the progress comment is marked finished

REQUIREMENT: RQCLAIM-6 On a failure, the label is removed and the progress comment is marked finished

REQUIREMENT: RQCLAIM-7 On an interrupt (TERM signal), the label is removed and the progress comment is marked finished

REQUIREMENT: RQCLAIM-8 A run with no issue (goal only) makes no claim

REQUIREMENT: RQLABEL-1 A local run and a CI run use the same label

REQUIREMENT: RQLABEL-2 There is no hostname in the label

LIMIT: LIMMECH-1 Do not build a check of a CI job's status through the GitHub Actions API
